title: New hypertrophy study just dropped (And Basically You're F*cking Stupid)
summary: He reviews a Jeff Nippard-led paper on optimal resistance training technique covering range of motion, tempo and technique, then adds practical nuance. He closes with a philosophical critique of 'optimal training' as a marketing claim, urging a student mindset without paralysis by analysis.
claims: Full range of motion tends to give more hypertrophy than partial range of motion
Lengthened partials may beat full ROM for hypertrophy, likely because you can use more load and reps in the stretched position
Hierarchy for hypertrophy: lengthened partials, then full ROM, then shortened partials
The ROM findings so far only have data for hamstrings, biceps and triceps
You don't need to lock out the elbow on triceps isolation; the lengthened part matters most, and he personally never locks out
Squeezing the contraction at the top seems to matter little for growth; removing that portion doesn't reduce hypertrophy
He predicts that for traps even zero ROM, just holding heavy weight in a stretch, may prove optimal
Prioritise full ROM and emphasise the lengthened bottom of the negative
Lighter weight through full ROM beat heavier weight with less ROM; settle and standardise ROM before loading the bar
Cutting ROM short to add weight is fake progress: you change the leverage, not your strength or size
Don't force ranges of motion you lack the mobility or leverage for; adjust per lift and body
Any tempo between 2 and 8 seconds per rep gave similar hypertrophy when load was adjusted to the tempo
Milo Wolf confirmed the tempo studies adjust load to tempo as standard methodology
You could cut load by about 30% and lift slower with similar hypertrophy (not strength)
As long as you control the eccentric for at least about 1 second rather than letting gravity drop it, tempo can follow preference
Very slow negatives are hard to standardise rep to rep; tempo drifts as you fatigue, which sabotages progressive overload
The tempo difference between a 2 s and a 6 s negative can be about 20 lb of load
Sets of 15 with 6-second negatives are long and boring, kill focus and intensity, and make fatigue hard to track
Adherence is the most important factor; if a method makes lifting a chore it becomes detrimental
If you like throwing weight around, a controlled 1-second negative gets similar results
Slow tempo with lighter weights can build mind-muscle connection for lifters who struggle to feel lats or chest, then you return to heavier loads
Slower tempo with lighter load likely reduces injury risk; useful when injured or dieting to keep tension without pain
His hierarchy: load as underlying condition (rank 0), then technique, ROM, tempo, and time under tension as a byproduct of tempo
Volume and intensity are the primary drivers of muscle growth; if the weight isn't challenging you won't grow
There is only one study on lifting technique, so questions like squat stance, elbow tuck or shoulder extension lack data
Curling with the elbow rising forward uses the shoulder to move more weight but gets less biceps; strict curls keep the elbow stationary
Cheat reps and body English let momentum, not the target muscle, move the weight; he considers them ego lifting
Fitness studies are best at telling you what not to do, not at defining one optimal technique
Letting the stack or your body drop uncontrolled on pulldowns or pull-ups hurts hypertrophy
Calling your method optimal or science-based is a prisoner's-dilemma marketing play that claims the high ground and shuts down criticism
Ontological manipulation, naming yourself so disagreement looks wrong by default, kills discussion in fitness and life
Natural plateaus are usually intellectual limits, not physical ones; the brain stops finding ways to grow
Natural lifters with great physiques are usually nerds obsessed with refining their training; become a student of the game
He is purely experience-based, never modified his training based on studies, and it never stopped him growing
He keeps partial preacher curls because they feel good on his tendons, he progresses and grows
He trains legs only with free weights and hip hinges despite evidence for leg curls and isolation
He dislikes lengthened partials: they feel clunky and make standardising sets and rep ranges harder
Theory is useless without application; the most important study is the one you run on yourself
About 90% of what works has been known for a century; new optimal research concerns the remaining 10% and mostly confirms the basics
Milo Wolf himself says lengthened partials help but not much and are dangerous to hyperfocus on
Hard sets are king; intensity techniques must never impede performance on hard sets
Avoid paralysis by analysis: pick a program and technique and go; anything B to S tier works
Most viewers are beginners who don't need optimisation; mistakes can be adjusted later
exercises: stop short of elbow lockout; emphasise the stretch
keep elbow stationary, don't let it rise forward
raising the elbow shifts work to the shoulder
comfortable on his tendons, he progresses on it
